## The idea

Second-order confirmatory factor models are often judged by fit indices
against fixed cutoffs. fitcheck asks three questions first, in a fixed order:

1. **Data.** Do the records contain real responses?
2. **Solution.** Is the estimated solution admissible?
3. **Fit.** Only then: what do the fit indices say, read with the unbiased
   SRMR and its interval?

A fourth step asks whether section scores deserve to be reported beside the
total score.

Each step is a separate function, so the checks can be added to an existing
lavaan analysis. The function `fitcheck()` runs all steps and returns one
report.

## Example data

The package ships with a simulated operational test: 2,000 records from three
forms, 80 dichotomous items in three sections (Listening 30, Grammar 20,
Reading 30), and 10 parcels. Some records were planted with every item scored
0, and some with a whole section scored 0, as happens with blank or partly
blank answer sheets.

```{r data}
library(fitcheck)
data(sim_test)
data(sim_test_design)
items <- sim_test[, sim_test_design$items]
str(sim_test_design$sections)
cat(sim_test_design$model)
```

## Check 0: the data

`screen_records()` flags two kinds of records: all-zero records and records
with a whole section scored 0. It flags; it does not delete.

```{r screen}
scr <- screen_records(items, sim_test_design$sections, form = sim_test$form)
scr
```

Can an all-zero record come from a real examinee who guessed? With four
options, the chance of scoring 0 on 30 items by blind guessing is very small:

```{r zero}
zero_probability(30)
```

Form B has far more flagged records than the other forms. In real data, a
pattern like this points to an administration or scanning problem rather than
to very weak examinees.

### Does screening matter?

`screening_sensitivity()` fits the same model with all records and with the
retained records only, and shows what changes.

```{r sensitivity}
keep <- scr$flags$keep
sens <- screening_sensitivity(items, keep, sim_test_design$parcels,
                              sim_test_design$model, std.lv = FALSE)
sens
```

The fit indices barely move, but the mean first-order loading and the omegas
change clearly. Records without real responses make the measurement look
stronger than it is, and the fit indices do not warn about this.

### Does screening matter in every form?

Flagged records are often concentrated in a few forms. `screening_by_form()`
repeats the comparison within each form, and `screening_invariance()` tests
configural, metric, and scalar invariance across forms with all records and
with the retained records.

```{r forms}
by_form <- screening_by_form(items, keep, sim_test$form,
                             sim_test_design$parcels, sim_test_design$model)
by_form[by_form$index == "mean_first_order_loading", ]
inv <- screening_invariance(items, keep, sim_test$form,
                            sim_test_design$parcels, sim_test_design$model)
inv
```

Screening changes form B much more than forms A and C, because form B holds
most of the flagged records. In these simulated data the invariance
conclusion is the same with and without the flagged records. In operational
data it can differ, and both results should then be reported. A second-order
model is tested through its correlated first-order version, which is
equivalent with three first-order factors.

### When screening changes the comparison of forms

In the data above, the invariance conclusion does not depend on screening. The
next example shows the opposite case. Three forms share the same 27 items and
the same loadings, so the forms are invariant by construction. The parcels
differ in difficulty (easy, medium, hard), as in many operational tests.
Adding 100 all-zero records to form B alone is enough to make metric
invariance fail with all records, while the retained records support scalar
invariance.

```{r forms2}
make_form <- function(n, seed) {
  set.seed(seed)
  p_correct <- rep(rep(c(.85, .60, .35), each = 3), 3)
  R <- matrix(.75, 3, 3); diag(R) <- 1
  F <- matrix(stats::rnorm(n * 3), n) %*% chol(R)
  Y <- sapply(1:27, function(j) {
    s <- (j - 1) %/% 9 + 1
    as.integer(.65 * F[, s] + sqrt(1 - .65^2) * stats::rnorm(n) > stats::qnorm(1 - p_correct[j]))
  })
  colnames(Y) <- paste0(rep(c("L", "G", "R"), each = 9), rep(1:9, 3))
  Y
}
X2 <- rbind(make_form(700, 1), make_form(700, 2), make_form(700, 3),
            matrix(0L, 100, 27))
form2 <- c(rep(c("A", "B", "C"), each = 700), rep("B", 100))
sections2 <- list(Listening = paste0("L", 1:9), Grammar = paste0("G", 1:9),
                  Reading = paste0("R", 1:9))
parcels2 <- list()
for (s in c("L", "G", "R")) for (p in 1:3) parcels2[[paste0(s, p)]] <- paste0(s, (p - 1) * 3 + 1:3)
model2 <- second_order_syntax(list(Listening = c("L1", "L2", "L3"),
                                   Grammar = c("G1", "G2", "G3"),
                                   Reading = c("R1", "R2", "R3")))
s2 <- screen_records(X2, sections2, form = form2)
screening_invariance(X2, s2$flags$keep, form2, parcels2, model2)
```

All-zero records lower easy parcels much more than hard parcels, so in form B
the parcels no longer follow the ratio of their loadings. A reader who saw
only the analysis with all records would conclude that the forms measure the
sections differently, although the difference comes from records without
real responses.

## Checks 1 to 4: the solution, then the fit

Fit the model to the parcel scores of the retained records with lavaan, then
run the four checks.

```{r checks}
d <- parcel_scores(items[keep, ], sim_test_design$parcels)
fit <- lavaan::cfa(sim_test_design$model, data = d, estimator = "MLR")
four_checks(fit)
```

Check 1 comes first: if the solution is not admissible (for example, a
negative variance), the fit indices below it describe a model that cannot be
interpreted, so they should not be read.

A negative disturbance variance can show up differently depending on how the
model is identified. `identification_check()` fits the model both ways.

```{r ident}
identification_check(sim_test_design$model, d)
```

For an admissible solution, `hierarchical_indices()` gives the omegas,
omega-hierarchical, and the explained common variance from the
Schmid–Leiman transformation.

```{r hier}
lapply(hierarchical_indices(fit), round, 3)
```

## How would the model behave in smaller samples?

`boot_by_n()` draws bootstrap samples of your own data at smaller sizes,
refits the model, and counts admissible, improper, and nonconverged solutions
separately. Every replication has its own pre-drawn seed, so the results are
identical on one core or several. Use 50 or more replications in practice;
10 keeps this example fast.

```{r boot}
boot_by_n(d, sim_test_design$model, ns = c(100, 300), reps = 10, seed = 1)
```

`mini_mc()` does the same from a population matrix, for example the matrix
implied by a fitted model:
`cov2cor(lavaan::lavInspect(fit, "implied")$cov)`.

## Do section scores add value?

`added_value()` compares how well a section score and the total score predict
the true section score (Haberman, 2008). The decision is based on a bootstrap
interval for the difference: *adds value*, *no added value*, or
*inconclusive*. `profile_check()` asks whether two section scores of one
examinee can be told apart.

```{r subscores}
av <- added_value(items[keep, ], sim_test_design$sections, B = 200, seed = 1)
av
profile_check(items[keep, ], sim_test_design$sections)
```

## Everything at once

```{r workflow}
report <- fitcheck(items, sim_test_design$sections, sim_test_design$parcels,
                   form = sim_test$form, B = 200)
report
```

If `model` is not given, `fitcheck()` builds a second-order model with one
first-order factor per section, measured by the parcels of that section.

## Limits

* **Parcels.** The workflow fits the model to parcel scores with robust
  maximum likelihood, because operational forms often have 80 or more items.
  Parcelling can hide item-level misfit. Item-level estimation of ordinal
  data (for example WLSMV) is a planned extension.
* **Screening is a judgment.** An all-zero record is flagged, not proven to
  be empty. `zero_probability()` helps judge how plausible a real all-zero
  score is, and the sensitivity table shows what the decision changes. The
  decision stays with the analyst.
* **Model family.** The checks are written for second-order models.
  `four_checks()` works for any lavaan fit, but `hierarchical_indices()`
  assumes one second-order factor.

## Related tools

fitcheck builds on known methods and does not replace the packages that
implement them. lavaan provides estimation, the admissibility check, and
`lavResiduals()` for the unbiased SRMR (Maydeu-Olivares, 2017). Omegas and
related indices are also available in semTools and psych; Haberman's
added-value statistics in subscore; simulation-based fit cutoffs in FCO.
fitcheck puts screening, admissibility, fit and score reporting in one order
and one report.

## References

Chen, F. F. (2007). Sensitivity of goodness of fit indexes to lack of
measurement invariance. *Structural Equation Modeling, 14*(3), 464–504.
https://doi.org/10.1080/10705510701301834

Haberman, S. J. (2008). When can subscores have value? *Journal of
Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 33*(2), 204–229.
https://doi.org/10.3102/1076998607302636

Maydeu-Olivares, A. (2017). Assessing the size of model misfit in structural
equation models. *Psychometrika, 82*(3), 533–558.
https://doi.org/10.1007/s11336-016-9552-7
